label: Gender history
scope: The existing gender entry is a teaching umbrella; these sources do not define its entire chronology or identify one unified school.
synthesis: Dialeti provides a way to examine the production of a canon itself: journal and regional coverage become questions for the review. The global companion provides a broader survey structure. Together they support moving beyond a sequence of celebrated theorists, but neither supplies a complete census of post-2000 contributions.
connections: Investigate the earlier Scott, Ghosh, Najmabadi and Stryker proposals alongside colonial, religious and intellectual histories. Keep feminist, gender, sexuality and trans interventions distinguishable when attributing claims.
gaps: Most new evidence here is abstract/description level. Reception, non-English surveys and the newest scholarship remain incomplete.
representation_question: Which historians and regional traditions disappear if discovery starts with highly cited Anglophone theorists? Does the selection recognize work outside established academic centres?
next_action: Read Dialeti’s regional comparisons, then sample companion chapters across regions and follow the cited historians into their substantive fields.

label: Disability history
scope: Disability is a provisional research-field referent, distinct from a diagnosis category, medical history, or a single rights-movement chronology.
synthesis: The state-of-field essay connects activism, social interpretation and mediated evidence of experience. The handbook provides a route to earlier and geographically wider histories. A dossier should retain the tension between recovering experience and relying on institutional sources.
connections: Check links with medical, social, labour, gender and colonial histories through named arguments; do not classify all histories of impairment as the same programme.
gaps: Selected opening passages and handbook description do not establish regional balance or developments after 2022.
representation_question: Whose experience and scholarship are missing when institutional and medical sources dominate? Audit women’s contributions and regional traditions without inferring scholars’ disability identities.
next_action: Read the survey’s bibliography and relevant handbook chapters, seeking independent histories beyond Anglo-American rights movements.

label: Borderlands history
scope: Keep borderlands distinct from frontier, transnational, Indigenous and imperial histories even when particular works connect them.
synthesis: The North American opening of On Borderlands emphasizes mobility and contested power. Van Schendel supplies a different regional and spatial problem: area-studies boundaries in Southeast Asia. This pair complicates a single frontier-origin story without demonstrating a comprehensive global genealogy.
connections: Investigate relationships with spatial, imperial and Indigenous histories using exact regional targets. A contribution to one borderland literature should not automatically target an umbrella for all borderlands.
gaps: The selected interventions are 2002 and 2011. A recent survey and 2020–2026 developments are outstanding, as are African and Latin American perspectives.
representation_question: Do male-dominated frontier narratives determine our shortlist before feminist and Indigenous scholarship is searched? Whose territorial categories structure the surveys?
next_action: Acquire a recent comparative survey and targeted feminist/Indigenous borderlands bibliographies before selecting people from the long Crossref list.

label: Digital history
scope: Digital history, computational history and digital humanities remain separate candidate identities; their relations require historical argument.
synthesis: Romein and colleagues make corpus construction and changing meanings methodological issues, not simply tool choices. Milligan’s broader treatment of digitization and search provides a route to ordinary research practice. These sources support distinguishing computational techniques from broader transformations in historical work.
connections: Examine older quantitative/computational traditions, source criticism and web history as specific connections. A cited tool or dataset does not establish a school or influence relation.
gaps: The extracted notes mix scholarship, software and commentary; they need parsing and relevance review. Institutional practices outside the surveyed Anglophone/European settings and 2023–2026 remain incomplete.
representation_question: Does a history of named technical pioneers erase collaborative, public-history or feminist contributions? The Leon chapter on the Great Man narrative is a concrete recovery lead, not yet read.
next_action: Read Leon’s chapter and recover named contributors from the surveys, while checking the distinction between authorship, technical labour and historical interpretation.

label: Web history
scope: Distinguish histories using archived web evidence from histories of the web itself; neither is interchangeable with all digital history.
synthesis: Brügger’s publisher description foregrounds the archived web as evidence and object. Milligan’s description foregrounds abundance and born-digital research problems. These are promising source-critical programmes but description-level checks cannot establish detailed disagreements or reception.
connections: Investigate digital history, media history, archival studies and contemporary history through passages on selection, loss and reconstruction of web records.
gaps: Both selected sources are publisher descriptions of 2018–2019 works. The saved handbook contents are discovery material, not read chapters; newer practice and non-Western web archives need coverage.
representation_question: Does starting with two prominent monographs hide women’s archival, collaborative and interpretive contributions? Which language communities become invisible through archive selection?
next_action: Use handbook chapters and archive-method scholarship to broaden the author pool, then read contrasting treatments of web archives and historical explanation.

label: History of emotions
scope: Emotions can be a field and an analytical category across fields; programme publication dates do not mark the beginning of emotional life or its historical study.
synthesis: The interview identifies several distinct analytical programmes; Scheer proposes embodied practice as another route. Their juxtaposition supplies questions about communities, regimes, norms and bodies, rather than grounds for collapsing them into one theory.
connections: Investigate cultural, social, gender and sensory histories, using direct discussion to identify adoption, disagreement or revision of particular concepts.
gaps: Both checks are abstracts from 2010–2012. Earlier roots, non-European traditions, reception and 2020–2026 interventions remain incomplete.
representation_question: Do famous concept names dominate selection at the expense of historians applying or challenging them? Audit the people selected for empirical and theoretical contributions alike.
next_action: Read the full interview and Scheer’s argument, then obtain a recent survey with regional and gender breadth before claiming a settled genealogy.

label: Sensory history
scope: A sensory approach crosses fields; a 2021 manifesto is an intervention, not a field-origin date.
synthesis: Smith’s introduction argues for sensory history as a wider historical practice. The taste/science abstract offers a specific knowledge-making problem. This pairing supports reading senses as historically organized practices rather than appending sensory details to existing narratives.
connections: Investigate emotions, material culture, medicine and knowledge history through arguments about embodiment and evidence. Shared vocabulary does not establish influence.
gaps: The checked introduction and abstract leave much of the multisensory and regional literature unread. The teaching bibliography is a discovery source and contains extraction boundaries needing repair.
representation_question: Do general manifestos obscure women’s work on particular senses, bodies and knowledge practices? Does a European sensory hierarchy become the assumed global frame?
next_action: Read taste/science case studies and a contrasting sensory survey; resolve the bibliography’s concatenated entries before counting works.

label: History of knowledge
scope: Knowledge is a provisional field referent with contested boundaries; do not absorb histories of science, information or the humanities into it automatically.
synthesis: The introductory programme and Daston’s boundary questions offer a productive disagreement about scope and coherence. Existing pilot circulation passages remain available through their exact claims. A very large bibliography should deepen these questions without giving this field disproportionate visual importance.
connections: Investigate science, information, education and humanities histories through specific disagreements about actors, practices and circulation.
gaps: Two selected works reuse existing pilot IDs. Provider references include malformed titles/authors; the 180 occurrences are not 180 verified works. Independent reception and non-European perspectives remain incomplete.
representation_question: Does canonical theory displace histories of everyday, gendered or colonized knowledge? Audit both who writes the histories and who becomes a historical knowledge actor without conflating the two.
next_action: Sample the bibliography alongside an independent regional survey; inspect Daston’s malformed Crossref references manually and retain source-level uncertainty.

label: Trans history
scope: The graph already has a trans intervention strand under queer history. This candidate review concerns scope and representation, not discovery of a wholly absent subject.
synthesis: Agarwal’s feature documents activist/academic exchanges and problems of historical identification. Hickman’s indexed excerpt proposes a taxonomy and competing starting points; the taxonomy remains her account. The dossier should keep disagreement about categories and temporal labels visible.
connections: Investigate queer, gender, medical, legal and activist histories through attributed claims. Do not infer identities of historical subjects or present-day scholars from the field they study.
gaps: The direct Hickman page was inaccessible; the full argument needs checking. The earlier Stryker edition evidence extends to 2026 but does not complete a recent field review.
representation_question: Which activist, trans and nonbinary contributions are lost by prioritizing conventional academic visibility? Demographic identities require evidence rather than inference from research topics.
next_action: Read the full review and contrasting regional histories; link the earlier Stryker proposals only after work and edition reconciliation.

label: Childhood and youth histories
scope: This is a joint research dossier, not a merger: childhood and youth retain separate candidate IDs. Current selected evidence chiefly addresses childhood; existing demographic-history strands are preserved.
synthesis: Tisdall connects childhood/adulthood categories with power and the limits of evidence about agency. The education article excerpt suggests a route through institutions and school-produced sources. Neither licenses treating youth as merely an older age band within a single universal developmental history.
connections: Investigate demographic, family, education, colonial and gender histories. Distinguish historians’ interventions from the years and ages they study.
gaps: The childhood survey’s notes include bundled citations, commentary and ibid references. Youth-specific surveys and later developments remain a material gap.
representation_question: Do developmental narratives privilege particular families, regions and institutions? Audit women’s scholarly contributions across childhood, education and youth rather than treating these as marginal specialties.
next_action: Acquire a youth-specific survey and follow the Global South leads in Tisdall’s notes; parse citation bundles without treating every note as a distinct work.

label: Memory studies and history
scope: Memory already has a full graph entry. Distinguish interdisciplinary memory studies from each historical argument and from the events remembered.
synthesis: Rothberg’s description supplies a proposal about relationships between Holocaust remembrance and decolonization. Erll’s metadata identifies a second reading but supplies no checked argument. The dossier therefore offers one provisional interpretive proposal and one explicit evidence gap.
connections: Investigate oral, public, cultural, Holocaust and colonial histories through passages about remembrance and reception. Similar topics or a suggestive title are insufficient evidence of conceptual borrowing.
gaps: No selected body text establishes the contrasting accounts, and 2020–2026 is unreviewed. The Crossref platform date for Rothberg is 2020; it must not replace the 2009 work date.
representation_question: Does a small group of famous theorists obscure women’s contributions and regional memory scholarship? Whose commemorative experiences and source languages define the shortlist?
next_action: Obtain Erll’s argument and Rothberg’s relevant passages, then select a recent independent survey before proposing a broader conceptual genealogy.

label: Transnational history
scope: Transnational history is an approach with several contexts, not a synonym for global, international or borderlands history.
synthesis: Saunier’s description provides an introductory route to connections across borders. The 2023 forum opening signals reassessment of what an emphasis on movement may obscure. Only the opening was checked, so specific contributors’ arguments remain to be read and separately attributed.
connections: Investigate global, international, imperial, migration and borderlands histories through contested units and scales of analysis.
gaps: The forum’s multi-author metadata does not authorize attributing its opening to every contributor. Regional trajectories, immobility and the full forum remain unreviewed.
representation_question: Do mobility-centred narratives privilege visible elite networks and their best-known historians? Search feminist and labour perspectives and record both their arguments and scholarly reception.
next_action: Read individual forum contributions and a contrasting regional survey; separate each contributor’s position before adding people or debate edges.
